questions.q: In the web app, does the browser read the repository, or does our server read it and hand the bytes on?
questions.lede: Zero document bytes in our control plane is the claim a server-side rival cannot copy, and the code breaks it in three places.

visual.note: F7 reads every markdown file by definition, so the first column breaks on an MVP-0 feature.
visual.caption: Three read shapes against GitHub's rate limit and the byte claim.

questions.stakes: Lose this and the web app is a hosted editor competing on features with free ones.
state: The week-0 draft proposes browser-side only: no document byte passes through a Zephyrus server (docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:35).

The code does the opposite. One operator token on every call (`src/shared/infrastructure/github/client.ts:30`), a whole-repo zipball (`client.ts:78`), and a server-parsed vault from `GET /api/vault/snapshot`.
The plan lists the byte path as `Decision` with no days (docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:221) and puts it in week 0 (docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:368).
path: The editor was forked from sgnk-md, a single-tenant hosted workspace that held documents by design.
An earlier round recommended the server lane: mint a 1-hour installation token, read a tarball (docs/research/agent-reports-2026-08-30/r20-q4-repo-and-folders.md:9).
The claim went into the architecture section later, and nobody reconciled it with the read path.
tension: The installation floor is 5,000 requests an hour and the founder's vault is 5,832 markdown files, so per-file reads cannot finish a whole-vault pass (r20-q4:38, :40).
The only whole-vault read that fits is a tarball, and 88.1 MB unzipped in a tab moves the cold-start problem rather than solving it.
Nothing here shows a browser can follow the zipball redirect to codeload; the draft admits one check is outstanding (docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:54).
Git-backed markdown editing is already free. Pages CMS is MIT with 3,976 stars and no paid tier, and it makes no claim about where the bytes go.

questions.lede: The headline artefact is a file in the user's repository, and on the web every review action is a repository write.

visual.note: On desktop this is one file write. On the web it is a git operation each time.

questions.stakes: Review state that is not written back is not durable across machines, which is the only form of the claim nothing observed reaches.
state: Exhibit 2 says review state on the web-GitHub lane is a sidecar committed with the files (docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:95).
The format is one JSON line per span in `.frontmatter/review.jsonl`, relocated by the splice locator on every edit (docs/PRODUCT-BRIEF.md:135).
Nothing specifies when that file is written on the web, or by what git operation.
path: On desktop the answer is obvious: write the file and let git see it. The web path was never separated from it.
The usage file hit the same wall and got a written decision (docs/WEEK0-DECISIONS-2026-09-08.md:20). The review file did not.
tension: Reading marks are generated far faster than edits, so a commit per action makes the history unreadable.
Batching loses state when a tab closes, on the surface AC2 recommends for the pilot.
Writes count against the same installation floor of 5,000 requests an hour as reads (r20-q4:38).
Durable in the repository, across sessions and machines, is the narrow form of the claim that survives. A browser-only cache is not that.

options.screens: None, until the user opens their own git log.

A commit per action turns the user's log into our telemetry, from a product that sells restraint.
(d) forfeits the one narrow claim nothing observed reaches, which is state durable across machines rather than per browser.
